fact_en: The wick is the part of a lamp that absorbs fuel and holds the flame.
fact_bis: Ang wick mao ang parte sa lampara nga mosuyop sa gasolina ug mogunit sa kalayo.

findings.note: Body: "Ang wick mao ang parte sa lampara nga mosuyop sa gasolina ug mogunit sa kalayo." The English says the wick absorbs *fuel* (generic); the Cebuano names gasolina = gasoline specifically, a different substance, and the card never corrects it. A lamp wick absorbs kerosene (gaas/petrolyo), never gasoline, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns a false — and household-unsafe — fact about lamps. Correct generic Cebuano would be sugnod/gatong, or gaas for a lamp.

fact_en: To describe reflection, we name the incoming light the incident ray, the bouncing light the reflected ray, and the imaginary line at a right angle to the mirror the normal line.
fact_bis: Aron ihulagway ang reflection, gitawag nato ang mosulod nga kahayag nga incident ray, ang mobutad nga kahayag nga reflected ray, ug ang imaginary nga linya nga patindog sa samin nga normal line.

findings.note: Definitional card naming the three rays of reflection. English "the bouncing light the reflected ray" becomes "ang mobutad nga kahayag nga reflected ray" — butad is to pull/stretch taut, never to bounce (should be mobalik/mobanda). The incident ray is correctly defined by contrast (mosulod = incoming) and the normal line is correct, so the reflected-ray definition is the card's load-bearing fact and nothing else in the Cebuano restores the sense of light bouncing off the mirror. A child reading only the Cebuano cannot say what a reflected ray is.

fact_en: Surface characteristics affect collision outcomes, so a ball bounces higher on hard concrete than on soft carpet.
fact_bis: Ang kinaiya sa surface nakaapekto sa resulta sa collision, busa mas taas molantaw ang bola sa gahi nga semento kaysa sa humok nga carpet.

findings.note: title_bis "Surface ug Lantaw" and the body "mas taas molantaw ang bola sa gahi nga semento kaysa sa humok nga carpet" use lantaw, which in Cebuano means TO LOOK / GAZE, not to bounce. Cebuano for bounce is motalbog (or molukso), and the rest of this corpus uses exactly that (dcard-07322 "motalbog sa mga butang", ffct-22860 "motalbog palayo", dcard-00344 "motalbog gikan sa bat"). Nothing else in the card restores the idea of bouncing: the title names the topic as "Surface and Looking", and the body's only statement about the ball is that it 'looks' higher on concrete. A child reading only the Cebuano cannot learn the card's single fact - that a ball bounces higher off hard concrete than off soft carpet - and cannot answer what the surface does to the ball.

fact_en:
How can you take care of the plants in your garden?

You can water them regularly, cultivate the soil, pull the weeds around them, and protect them from stray animals.
fact_bis:
Giunsa nimo pag-atiman ang mga tanom sa imong tanaman?

Mahimo nimo silang bisbisan kanunay, lugdangon ang yuta, ibton ang mga sagbot libot kanila, ug panalipdan sila batok sa mga stray animals.

findings.note: EN: "cultivate the soil" (one of four plant-care steps). BIS: "lugdangon ang yuta" — lugdang = to SINK / SETTLE to the bottom (all 50 other corpus uses are sediment/precipitate/denser-liquid settling); tilling is bungkagon/kalotan ang yuta. The instruction inverts into "make the soil settle", i.e. compact it — the opposite of loosening — and the card never corrects it.

fact_en: Larvae hatch from eggs but do not look like adult insects, and they grow quickly enough to molt several times before pupating.
fact_bis: Ang larvae mapusa gikan sa itlog apan dili parehas sa mga adult nga insekto, ug paspas silang motubo mao nga makatulo ka beses silang mag-molt sa dili pa mahimong pupa.

findings.note: EN: larvae "molt several times before pupating". BIS: "makatulo ka beses silang mag-molt" = molt THREE times — a vague quantity turned into a specific wrong count (most larvae molt 4-5+ instars). Elsewhere the corpus renders "several times" as balik-balik / sa makadaghang higayon, and uses makatulo ka beses for a literal 3x (ffct-27631). Unrecoverable from the card.

fact_en: Plants need water to grow, and when they do not get enough water, their leaves turn yellow and wither.
fact_bis: Ang mga tanom nagkinahanglan ug tubig aron motubo, ug kon kulang sila sa tubig, manago ug malaya ang ilang mga dahon.

findings.note: EN: leaves "turn yellow and wither". BIS: "manago ug malaya ang ilang mga dahon" — manago = to HIDE, not to turn yellow (Cebuano is modalag/manilaw; the same corpus uses modalag for exactly this in ffct-04473). Half the card's two-symptom fact is replaced by a nonsense action and nothing else in the one-sentence card restores it: a Cebuano-only child learns leaves "hide", and cannot say what colour water-starved leaves turn.

fact_en:
How do butterflies taste leaves?

Adult butterflies have special taste receptors on their feet, which they use to taste leaves before laying their eggs there.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtilaw sa paru-paro sa dahon?

Ang mga hamtong nga paru-paro adunay espesyal nga sensory receptors sa ilang tiil aron matilawan ang dahon una sila mangitlog didto.

findings.note: title_bis 'Titi sa Tiil sa Alibangbang' for title_en "Butterflies' Tasting Feet". 'Titi' is not the Cebuano for taste (tilaw/timtim) and reads as the vulgar term for penis — unacceptable in a grade-school card title, and the title as written conveys no meaning. Body is fine ('adunay espesyal nga sensory receptors sa ilang tiil aron matilawan ang dahon una sila mangitlog didto'), so the fact itself survives; the defect is the title word. Standalone 'titi' occurs in only 3 cards corpus-wide, all apparent artifacts (ffct-00424 'Prints sa Titi ug Palad' for 'Prints on Toes and Palms'; ffct-02351 'Laing Prints Titi'), so the grep pair is narrow.

fact_en: Germs can spread through dirty water or food with bacteria and cause diarrhea — boiling water, washing fruit, and cooking food well can stop this.
fact_bis: Mokatap ang mga germs sa hugaw nga tubig o pagkaon nga adunay bacteria ug makahatag og kalibanga — mapugngan kini pinaagi sa pagpabukal sa tubig, paghugas sa prutas, ug husto nga pagluto.

findings.note: title_bis 'Kalainan sa Tubig ug Pagkaon' = 'the DIFFERENCE between water and food', but the card is 'Germs in Food and Water' (tl title is 'Kalusugan sa Tubig at Pagkain'). 'Kalainan' is used in its ordinary 'difference' sense in ~20 other corpus titles (e.g. 'Kalainan sa Pond ug Lanaw' = Pond vs Lake), so this is not a regional reading of 'lain' as 'bad' — the title announces a comparison the card never makes. Not given as a word-pair because greping 'kalainan' corpus-wide would be almost all fine.

fact_en: A snail leaves behind a shiny trail of slime as it crawls.
fact_bis: Ang kuhol magbilin ug sinaw nga agi sa uhog samtang kini magkamang.

findings.note: title_bis 'Daug nga Lika sa Kuhol' for 'Snail Slime Trail' names neither slime nor trail: 'daug' means win/defeat and 'lika' is not slime (uhog) or track (agi). The title is the only place a child sees the topic named, and it points at nothing. 'Daug' is used the same way as 'trail/track' in two other corpus titles (ffct-08253 Dugong Feeding Trails, ffct-09038 Herd Footprint Fossils), so the grep is small and targeted. Body sentence itself is correct ('sinaw nga agi sa uhog').

fact_en:
What really causes sore muscles after exercise?

It's not lactate! When muscles work without enough oxygen they make lactate, but the soreness you feel later actually comes from tiny muscle tears and inflammation.
fact_bis:
Unsa gyud ang hinungdan sa kasakit sa kaunuran human mag-ehersisyo?

Dili ang lactate! Kon ang kaunuran magtrabaho nga walay igo nga oxygen, maghimo kini og lactate, apan ang kasakit nga imong gibati tungod sa gagmay nga luha sa kaunuran ug inflammation.

findings.note: "ang kasakit nga imong gibati tungod sa gagmay nga luha sa kaunuran" — English "tiny muscle tears" (rips) rendered as "luha" (teardrops, the crying kind). This is the card's whole answer: it's not lactate, it's micro-tears + inflammation. With "luha" the real cause is never stated anywhere on the card, so the child cannot answer the question the card asks. Classic English homograph trap; "luha" is never right for tears-as-rips.

fact_en:
How does the pangolin help the forest?

By eating millions of ants and termites every year, it keeps their populations in balance in the forest!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtabang sa pangolin sa lasang?

Pinaagi sa pagkaon og milyun-milyong langgam ug termite matag tuig, napabalanse niini ang ilang populasyon sa lasang!

findings.note: Body says the pangolin eats "milyun-milyong langgam ug termite" — in Cebuano langgam = BIRD, not ant (ant = hulmigas). English is "millions of ants and termites". Nothing in the card corrects it, so a Cebuano-only reader learns that pangolins eat millions of birds. Confirmed in-corpus: every other card in this batch uses langgam for bird (ffct-00339 "Langgam ba ang kabog?", ffct-00345, ffct-00380, ffct-00412) and ffct-00398 uses hulmigas for ant.

title_bis: Prints sa Tudlo sa Tiil ug Palad
fact_en:
Do only fingers have unique prints?

Nope — your toes, palms, and even the soles of your feet each have their own one-of-a-kind pattern too!
fact_bis:
Tudlo ra ba ang adunay kaugalingong guhit?

Dili diay — ang mga tudlo sa tiil, palad, ug lapalapa adunay usab kaugalingong sumbanan nga walay sama!

findings.note: title_bis "Prints sa Titi ug Palad" for title_en "Prints on Toes and Palms". "Titi" is not toes (tudlo sa tiil) — it is the vulgar word for penis in Cebuano/Tagalog, and it stands as the headline on a grade-school card about fingerprints. The body is correct ("tudlo sa tiil, palad, ug lapalapa"), so the fact survives, but the title names a different body part and is obscene in a kids' app. Grep "titi" corpus-wide.
